analytic.title: A Fair Scheduling Algorithm and Schedulability Analysis for Performance Asymmetric Multiprocessors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: We propose a new scheduling policy for performance asymmetric multiprocessors that have identical instruction sets but different processing speeds. The difference between it and the original Pfair scheduling is that when selecting scheduling parameters such as the pseudo deadline of the subtask and selecting the processor when running the highest priority subtask, it can be aware of the performance asymmetry of the underlying processor. In addition, we also propose a sufficient schedulability test for Pfair scheduling on performance asymmetric multiprocessors.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In recent years, with the rapid development of multi-core processors, research into real-time scheduling algorithms in multiprocessor systems has become a hot topic. Task scheduling on multiprocessors has been continuously addressing two problems, namely task allocation and priority assignment. Real-time scheduling algorithms based on task allocation can be classified into three categories, global scheduling, local scheduling, and hybrid scheduling. Global scheduling refers to processors fetching tasks from a global queue, allowing tasks to migrate between processors at runtime. Local scheduling [1] refers to pre-allocating a task queue for each processor, prohibiting tasks from migrating between processors during runtime. Combining these two scheduling methods and assigning tasks to queues corresponding to different clusters, then employing a quasi-global scheduling algorithm within the cluster, is termed as hybrid scheduling. Related studies have proven that these three scheduling methods are all NPhard problems in multiprocessor scheduling, so approximate optimal solutions can only be obtained through optimization algorithms.

Real-time systems play a pivotal role in contemporary technology, spanning various domains, from wireless communication to embedded control systems. These systems are essential for ensuring that tasks and processes meet their time constraints, all while requiring equitable distribution of computational resources to meet the diverse needs of different tasks. In this dynamic and diverse environment, ensuring fair resource allocation among tasks has become particularly crucial to prevent performance imbalances and task starvation. Asymmetric multiprocessors can achieve better performance and energy efficiency. In order to make full use of the advantages of performance improvement and power consumption reduction brought by this architecture, it is necessary to implement appropriate scheduling and task allocation methods at the operating system level. In [2], two real-time task allocation methods based on the EDZL scheduling strategy have been proposed. The choice between these two methods depends on the selection of processor speeds. In [3], the task allocation problem on asymmetric multiprocessing systems is first considered.

The proportional fair scheduling algorithm is a typical global scheduling algorithm [4], known for effectively enhancing system utilization, especially in scenarios involving periodic task sets with implicit deadlines. The root of many studies on this topic stem from the pioneering work of Baruah et al. in proportional fairness [5]. The Pfair scheduling algorithm aims to achieve proportional fairness, which means that each task or process should receive an equitable share of resource allocation and not be ignored due to the specific requirements of certain tasks.

In order to make full use of the advantages of both, we propose a PA-Pfair (Performance Asymmetric Pfair) scheduling policy for performance asymmetric multiprocessors that have identical instruction sets but different processing speeds. We also obtain a new schedulability test for the PA-Pfair on performance asymmetric multiprocessors.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In section 2, We describe the background of Pfair scheduling. In section 3, we describe the system models and definitions. In section 4, we propose the PA-Pfair scheduling algorithm. In section 5, we provide a brief overview of the EDF scheduling algorithm.
In section 6, we describe PA-Pfair schedulability analysis for performance asymmetic multiprocessor platform.

div.head: II. BACKGROUND
div.p: The Pfair algorithm is a shared resource fair scheduling algorithm proposed by Baruah et al. [5] for real-time periodic tasks. Due to the high cost of this algorithm in practical applications, they divided tasks into light and heavy tasks based on their weights and proposed the pseudo deadline (PD) algorithm.

Anderson et al. [6] proposed the P D 2 algorithm by adding the concept of group time limit parameters on the basis of the PD algorithm, and proved that its scheduling cycle task set is optimal. Later, they further proved that the Pfair scheduling algorithm can solve the optimal scheduling problem for periodic tasks on multiprocessors in polynomial time. Anderson et al. [7] proposed the ER-fair algorithm on the basis of improving the P D 2 algorithm. ER-fair allows subtasks to be released before their runtime window, meaning that if two subtasks are subtasks of the same task, the another subtask is allowed to execute when the first subtask is completed. Pfair scheduling is slightly different from traditional real-time scheduling methods, and its tasks clearly need to be executed at a stable rate [8]. Moulik et al. [9] effectively reduced the task migration problem in multiprocessor systems by leveraging the advantages of the ER air algorithm. Nelissen et al. [10] summarized and categorized all proportional fair scheduling algorithms and their enhancements. Calandrino and his colleagues proposed several auxiliary algorithms aimed at reducing the overhead in the task priority assignment process for proportional fair scheduling algorithms [11]. In subsequent research, improved algorithms based on genetic algorithms have been proposed to alleviate the excessive overhead issues arising from the subsequent allocations of the Pfair scheduling algorithm [12].

The Pfair scheduling algorithm has also been extensively expanded and applied in many aspects. Katila et al. [13] combined the Pfair algorithm with the discrete uniform distribution algorithm to effectively solve the fairness problem of network scheduling. Kim et al. [14] demonstrated that the Pfair algorithm is the most widely used scheduling algorithm for multiprocessors, and combined this algorithm to solve the problem of time fairness in the global scheduling process of Linux fully fair schedulers.

The Pfair scheduling algorithm believes that in one period, each periodic task τ i (C i , D i ) is composed of C i subtasks µ k and each subtask has an execution time unit. A subtask µ k = (r k , d k , w k ) is characterized by a release time or earliest scheduling time r k , a deadline d k , and w k is the scheduling window within which subtasks must be scheduled by the processor. All subtasks of waiting for scheduling forms a global waiting queue in priority order, and when new subtasks arrive, they are inserted into the waiting queue according to priority. The processor checks the waiting queue at each time point and selects m subtasks with higher priority for scheduling. Pfair is a global scheduling algorithm where each subtask can run on different processors, and all tasks in the system wait fairly for processor scheduling.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODELS AND DEFINITIONS
div.p: Real-time systems are usually modeled as a finite set of independent cyclic tasks, and each task generates a potentially infinite job sequence. In this paper, we consider a sporadic task model. Let Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } be a set of n sporadic tasks, a sporadic τ i is defined by

div.p: where C i is the worst-case execution time based on the slowest processor speed, D i is the relative deadline,and T i is minimum inter-release time , which is also referred as period of the task.
In order to understand our system model, some attributes and parameters are very convenient.
We refer to the ratio of C i and T i as the weight of task denoted by ω t (i).The ω t (i) is defined as follows:
div.formula: ω t (i) = C i T i(1)
div.p: We consider m-core performance asymmetric multiprocessors and use π = {P 1 , P 2 , . . . , P m } to denote a set of such processors. The processors are labeled in non-decreasing order of processing speed. We use s i to represent the processing speed of each processor P i ; s i ≤ s i+1 . For national convenience, we use 1 to represent the speed of the slowest processor, such that the speed of faster processors can be represented by a multiple 1; for example, s i = 2. Let Y p be the cumulative speed of the first p processors in a performance asymmetric multiprocessors platform π . It is denoted as:

div.p: For a uniform multiprocessor platform with m processors, the value range of this parameter is between 0 and (m -1).
When all processors have the same processing speed (i.e., the platform is the uniform multiprocessor), the value (m-1) corresponds to the degradation case.

The least common multiple (LCM ) represents the minimum common multiple of all periodic tasks within the task set, denoted as LCM , which is the hyperperiod of this task set. If the task set can be executed within its hyperperiod without missing deadlines, it indicates that the task set is schedulable.

IV. PA-PFAIR SCHEDULING ALGORITHM We proposed PA-Pfair scheduling algorithms is based on the assumption that tasks(parts of them) can be executed on any processor and that tasks can be suspended on one processor and resumed on another at any time. In other words, tasks must be able to migrate between processors if necessary [18].

The proposed PA-Pfair scheduling divides each task into unit-sized subtasks. PA-Pfair associates each subtask with a new release time and deadline, called pseudo-release time and pseudo-deadline. The time interval determined by the pseudorelease time and pseudo-deadline is called the time window. To satisfy the fairness constraint, each subtask must execute within its associated time window. At runtime, it chooses the highest priority subtask and executes it on the fastest processor. Different subtasks of a task can be executed on different processors (i.e., inter-processor migration is permitted), but may not execute simultaneously (i.e., parallelism is prohibited).

The research in this article requires making fundamental assumptions about the tasks, which are outlined as follows:(1) the execution time C i of the task does not exceed its period T i , (2) the task has an implicit deadline, i.e., D i = T i .
Introduce some new concepts in the Pfair algorithm. Here are some related terms and explanations.

div.head: A. Execution windows
div.p: We denote the j th subtask of task τ i as µ i,j , where j ≥ 1. Each task can execute within the execution window specified by its pseudo-release time and deadlines denoted by r (µ i,j ) and d (µ i,j ), respectively.
div.formula: r (µ i,j ) = j -1 ω t (τ i )(6)
d (µ i,j ) = j ω t (τ i )(7)
div.p: Each subtask must run within the window defined by its release time and deadline.

Based on the described system model, figure1 illustrates the first five execution windows of task τ i with implicit deadlines. Each subtask of task τ i runs within its own window. At each time instant t, the PA-Pfair scheduling algorithm first determines which subtasks can be executed and then allocates them to the currently available processors. If a subtask τ i,j of τ i is within the execution window and the preceding subtask τ i,j-1 has already been executed, then the task can be scheduled at time t.
If two subtasks have the same deadline or overlapping execution windows, we need to add an additional parameter called the successor bit.

div.head: C. Priority assignment and subtask allocation
div.p: Firstly, we need to calculate the release time, deadline, and successor bit parameters for each subtask separately. We assign priority to subtasks based on EDF (earliest deadline first scheduling algorithm will be mentioned in the next section), and the earlier the deadline, the higher its priority. When subtasks have the same deadlines, we compare the successor bits(i.e.b (µ i,j )) and assign high priorities to tasks with large successor bit values. div.head: EDF SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
div.p: A set of n periodic tasks Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } is executed on the system.A periodic task is defined as a triple, τ i = (C i , D i , T i ), where C i is the worst-case execution time, D i is the relative deadline,and T i is the arrival period of a periodic task. A task can generate an infinite sequence of jobs, with a minimum arrival interval of one period between consecutive jobs.

The current job j i of task τ i is released at time r i , with an absolute deadline of d i ; the current job j j of task τ j has an absolute deadline of d j . If d i < d j , job j i has a higher priority than job j j ; conversely, if d i > d j , job j j has a higher priority than job j i . A real-time scheduling algorithm that prioritizes tasks according to this method of assigning priorities is called the Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling algorithm.

The priority assignment in the EDF scheduling algorithm is based on the job's absolute deadline, with jobs having smaller absolute deadlines being assigned higher priorities. EDF scheduling has been proven as an optimal algorithm. Specifically, if any other dynamic algorithm ensures no task deadlines are missed, employing the EDF algorithm will also guarantee that tasks meet their deadlines without any being missed. When a task's deadline equals its period, the sufficient and necessary condition for schedulability is that the total utilization of the task set is less than or equal to 1.

div.head: Fig. 2. EDF algorithm
div.p: Figure 2 illustrates a straightforward scenario employing the EDF (Earliest Deadline First) algorithm. This example comprises four periodic tasks arriving sequentially. Initially, the system schedules and executes task 1, the earliest arrival. While task 1 is in progress, tasks 3 and 4 arrive subsequently. As the deadline for task 4 precedes that of task 3, the system, after completing task 1, prioritizes and executes task 4. During the execution of task 4, task 2 arrives, maintaining its deadline earlier than that of task 3. Consequently, upon the completion of task 4, the system schedules the execution of task 2, followed by the eventual execution of task 3.

div.head: VI. PA-PFAIR SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS FOR PERFORMANCE ASYMMETRIC MULTIPROCESSOR PLATFORM
div.p: Schedulability analysis is an important part of real-time system research.If a multiprocessor system is capable of scheduling a task set, then each task within that set must satisfy its deadline requirement within its scheduling period [19]. This criterion stands as both a sufficient and necessary condition for the schedulability of a task set.

On a performance asymmetric multiprocessor platform, the given task set is called PA-Pfair schedulable if the deadline of all subtasks of the task can be met. Then we will derive the schedulability analysis of PA-Pfair on performance asymmetric multiprocessors. Assuming that in a global priority queue composed of all subtasks, the last subtask misses its deadline at time instant d i , see figure 3. During the first supercycle of all tasks, the last subtask in the global subtask ready queue missed its deadline. Based on this situation, we first obtain the necessary condition for the it to miss the deadline under PA-Pfair scheduling. By taking the inverse proposition of this condition, a sufficient schedulability condition is obtained. If this condition is met, we believe that the task set can be scheduled by PA-Pfair on the performance asymmetric multiprocessor. Figure 4 illustrates an example of a task set that is not schedulable. Assuming there are five tasks, three processors, and the last subtask in a queue composed of 19 subtasks misses its deadline at the time instant t(i.e., the hyperperiod of these five tasks).

We derive the necessary condition for the last subtask to miss the deadline are as follows:(1) Deriving the lower bound of the total processor time requirement within the time interval (0, d i ). (2) Deriving the upper bound of the total processor time requirement within the time interval (0, d i ).
(3) Combining the lower and upper bounds as a necessary condition for meeting the PA-Pfair scheduling.

div.head: B. Upper Bound
div.p: Now, we try to derive the upper bound of the total processor time requirement within the time interval (0, d i ). For this situation, we need to consider two types of tasks: completed tasks that all subtasks have been executed and completed, and common task that last subtask missed the deadline at time d i . We use R r and R c to represent the total processor time requirements for common tasks and completed tasks, respectively.

Let's first consider the upper bound of R c . When the last subtask in the global queue missed its deadline, all subtasks of other tasks have completed their execution process. Within this interval, there may have been multiple periodic executions of tasks completed. In order to relax our restrictions, we only consider the execution time of each task within one period in this interval. We use R c to represent the sum of processor time requirements for all completed and executed tasks within this interval in one period. So we have

Secondly, let's consider the upper bound of the total processor time requirement caused by common tasks. It is a well researched topic and the algorithm is famous for calculating DBF and LOAD [15,20]. Baruah et al indicates that the upper bound of R r can be calculated by ∆ × LOAD (Γ) [3]. ∆ is the interval length of certain period of time.
As a result, the upper bound of the total processor time requirement can be expressed as
div.formula: R (0, d i ) ≤ LOAD (Γ) ∆ + R c(19)
div.p: Based on the ( 17) and ( 19), We can obtain the necessary conditions for the task set to miss the deadline under PA-Pfair scheduling
div.formula: Y m d i -λ (π) C i ≤ LOAD (Γ) ∆ + R c(20)

div.head: C. PA-Pfair Schedulability Test
div.p: We are now describing a schedulability test for our PA-Pfair scheduling algorithm.

Theorem 1: A task set Γ = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } is schedulable by PA-Pfair on a m-core performance asymmetric multiprocessor platform π = {P 1 , P 2 , . . . , P m },with processing speeds s i ≤ s i+1 , if it statisfies the following condition
div.formula: Y m d i -λ (π) C i ≥ LOAD (Γ) ∆ + R c(21)
div.p: Proof of Theorem 1: We use the principle of contradiction to prove it. We have obtained a necessary condition that the task set cannot be fully scheduled under PA-Pfair scheduling. Taking this condition as the opposite, we can obtain the sufficient condition for the schedulability of PA-Pfair. As stated in theorem 1.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSION
div.p: In this paper, we proposed a fair scheduling approach for asymmetric multiprocessing systems, where task prioritization is based on the EDF algorithm. It involves partitioning each task into multiple subtasks based on execution time requirements, ensuring that each subtask receives processor scheduling as close as possible to its deadline. This method effectively reduces long-term resource wastage for a particular task in contrast to traditional EDF algorithms. Furthermore, leveraging the introduced PA-Pfair characteristics, we established a comprehensive schedulability test for fair scheduling on asymmetric multiprocessing systems. In future, our work can be extended to minimize task migrations and enhance task response times.
